Family Health

Understanding ovarian cancer stages, substages and survival statistics

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A stage tells the care team where ovarian cancer has been found and helps guide treatment. A survival percentage describes a group of people. Neither is a complete prediction of one person’s future. Understanding the labels can make reports easier to discuss, especially when different websites appear to give different answers.

Begin with the exact cancer type

The main groups arise from different kinds of cells. Epithelial cancers involve cells lining the ovaries or fallopian tubes and make up most ovarian cancers. Stromal cancers arise from supporting tissue that can produce hormones. Germ-cell cancers arise from cells involved in forming eggs.

These groups have different features and treatment pathways. Borderline and benign ovarian tumours are also distinct from invasive cancer. Ask for the precise pathology diagnosis rather than using any article about an ovarian lump as if it applies to every tumour.

Related cancers may share a staging system

Epithelial ovarian cancer, fallopian tube cancer and primary peritoneal cancer are closely related and are commonly considered together for staging and treatment. The peritoneum is the lining of the abdominal cavity and its organs. The original site and the exact tumour type still belong in the written diagnosis.

A page may use ovarian cancer as shorthand while its evidence includes related cancers. Check the stated population, especially before comparing outcomes. A germ-cell tumour should not automatically be assigned the outlook of a common invasive epithelial tumour.

Stage and grade answer different questions

Stage describes the extent of disease. Grade concerns the appearance of the cells and can help describe their likely behaviour; grading systems vary with tumour type. A higher grade is not the same as a higher stage, and the size of the main ovarian mass alone does not determine either.

Reports may use FIGO stages or the related TNM system. TNM records the tumour’s extent, lymph-node involvement and distant spread. Ask the team to explain the combined stage and its supporting findings rather than trying to translate an isolated letter from a scan report.

How a clinical or surgical stage is established

Examination, imaging, biopsy and other pathology information contribute to assessment. Surgery can reveal the extent of disease and provide samples from different sites. When surgery is not the first step, the team may discuss a clinical stage based on the information available before it.

Ask whether the stage is provisional and what further results could refine it. Symptoms alone cannot establish a stage: pain does not necessarily mean distant spread, and feeling well does not rule it out. Bring the actual report to an appointment if wording seems inconsistent.

Stage I: confined to the ovary or fallopian tube

IA means disease is confined to one ovary or tube; IB involves both. For these substages, the ovarian capsules are intact, surfaces are clear and abdominal fluid or washings contain no malignant cells.

IC adds particular findings despite confinement to one or both ovaries or tubes: IC1 is spill during surgery; IC2 is rupture before surgery or surface tumour; IC3 is malignant cells in abdominal fluid or washings. The timing and location of a finding therefore matter, not just the word rupture.

Stage II: spread within the pelvis

Stage II involves pelvic extension. IIA concerns extension or deposits involving the uterus, tubes or ovaries. IIB involves other tissues within the pelvic peritoneal cavity.

The distinction is anatomical. A mention of the bladder or bowel needs interpretation of the exact site and extent, rather than assuming any bowel-related symptom means stage II. Ask the specialist to point out the relevant findings on a diagram or report.

Stage III: abdominal lining beyond the pelvis or regional nodes

IIIA1 means spread to retroperitoneal lymph nodes only beyond the ovarian/tubal or pelvic disease. Its subdivisions use the largest nodal cancer deposit: IIIA1(i) is 10 mm or less and IIIA1(ii) is larger than 10 mm. IIIA2 means microscopic peritoneal spread above the pelvic brim, with or without involved retroperitoneal nodes.

IIIB means visible peritoneal deposits beyond the pelvis measuring no more than 2 cm. IIIC means deposits larger than 2 cm and includes involvement of the liver or spleen capsule without growth inside those organs. Retroperitoneal nodes may be involved in either IIIB or IIIC.

Stage IV: distant spread

IVA means malignant cells are found in fluid around the lungs. Fluid alone does not establish this substage; the finding of cancer cells matters. IVB includes spread inside liver or spleen tissue, to organs outside the abdomen, or to specified distant lymph nodes.

Cancer on the liver’s outer covering is classified differently from cancer growing within liver tissue. This is one reason the phrase spread to the liver is not enough to assign a stage. Stage IV does not by itself mean that treatment or supportive care is unavailable.

Registry groups are not a one-to-one FIGO translation

Survival reports often use localized, regional and distant categories. These are broader registry groupings describing whether disease is confined to its original site, has nearby spread or has more distant spread. They are not a table of every FIGO stage and substage.

Do not simply relabel localized as I, regional as II–III and distant as IV. For example, some abdominal peritoneal spread is FIGO III even though it can fall within a registry’s distant category. Use a statistic only with the definition used by the dataset, not a convenient conversion.

What five-year relative survival measures

Relative survival compares observed survival in people with a cancer diagnosis with expected survival in a comparable general population. The five-year figure is a measurement at a chosen point after diagnosis, not a limit on lifespan or a statement that treatment lasts five years.

For a simple illustration, suppose 60% of a cancer cohort and 80% of a comparable population were alive at that point. Relative survival would be 60 divided by 80, or 75%. Those invented numbers show the calculation only; they are not ovarian cancer estimates.

A dated comparison by cancer type

The following five-year relative survival estimates come from the American Cancer Society’s US SEER tables for diagnoses in 2015–2021, revised August 8, 2025 and checked for this review. The order in each line is localized, regional, distant, then all stages combined.

Invasive epithelial ovarian cancer: 92%, 71%, 32%, 51%.

Ovarian stromal tumours: 96%, 88%, 75%, 91%.

Ovarian germ-cell tumours: 98%, 94%, 76%, 93%.

Fallopian tube cancer: 92%, 66%, 40%, 54%.

These categories and diagnosis years are essential to interpreting the figures. They are not estimates for every country or an individual FIGO substage, and the four groups should not be blended into one personal prediction.

One-year and ten-year figures ask different questions

Survival measured from diagnosis to one, five or ten years uses different follow-up periods. Being alive one year after diagnosis is not the same question as the chance of living another five years after already surviving that first year. The latter requires an appropriate conditional-survival analysis.

Do not fill the gaps between published figures by guessing, or use a table without its population, method and diagnosis years. A year-by-year curve may be useful if the team can identify a suitable dataset. A list of percentages without that context can look precise while answering the wrong question.

Treatment changes and incidence trends need separate interpretation

Survival datasets necessarily describe people diagnosed earlier. Current care may differ from the care available in those years, so older figures may not fully reflect the options offered today. That is a reason to ask about current treatment, not a guarantee that every person’s outlook is better by a known amount.

Incidence means the rate of new diagnoses in a population. A fall in new cases over time is different from an improvement in survival among people who already have cancer. Historical incidence trends should not be used to calculate an individual’s prognosis or interpreted without a defined country and period.

Your own outlook involves more than stage

The care team considers tumour type and grade, general health, the amount of disease, what can be removed, response to treatment and relevant molecular or inherited findings. Some factors become clearer only after testing or treatment. Group statistics cannot capture all of that information.

Tell the team how much numerical information you want. Some people prefer ranges and detailed discussion; others want to understand the next decision first. You can return to the topic later, ask for written explanations or bring someone to help take notes.

Questions to bring before treatment

Ask: What is the exact type, grade and stage? Which findings establish it? Are further tests needed before we decide? What are the recommended options, their goals and likely duration? Would additional genetic or tumour testing change the plan?

Also ask about side effects and how to manage them, the contact route between appointments and whether a clinical trial is relevant. Raise fertility, menopause, sexual health and practical support needs before treatment when possible. They are part of care, not distractions from the cancer diagnosis.

Plan follow-up and ask about new concerns

Before leaving an appointment, clarify what happens next, who will contact you with results and when to call if you have not heard. After treatment, ask what follow-up is planned and which symptoms or changes should prompt an earlier review. Do not create a monitoring schedule from a survival chart.

Cancer that returns or progresses needs a new clinical discussion; a statistic grouped by stage at first diagnosis cannot simply be reassigned as a forecast for recurrence. Keep copies of reports and questions, and use the team’s urgent contact instructions for new or worsening symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

FIGO substages describe anatomical spread and specific pathology findings. The NCI professional staging tables were checked alongside patient guidance; stage, grade and the diameter of the original mass remain distinct concepts.

Numerical survival comparisons are explicitly limited to the cited US SEER cohorts and definitions. The earlier unverified one-to-ten-year series is not republished or reconstructed. Relative-survival figures describe populations, not individual deadlines or treatment eligibility.

How BeMama can help

Keep the diagnosis, questions and upcoming steps together. Ask the oncology team to explain one unfamiliar term at a time and to relate evidence to the actual pathology and treatment plan.

When to seek help

This guide cannot diagnose or assign a cancer stage. Use your cancer team’s instructions for urgent symptoms and treatment complications, and seek prompt medical care for severe or rapidly worsening illness.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Cancer type, stage and grade each provide different information.
  • Substage details include fluid cytology, where deposits are found and their size.
  • Liver-surface involvement differs from cancer inside liver tissue.
  • Registry survival groups are not interchangeable with FIGO stages.
  • Dated population figures cannot predict one person’s future or replace a treatment discussion.

Frequently asked questions

Is grade 3 the same as stage III?

No. Grade concerns cell features and behaviour, while stage describes the extent of disease. Ask which grading system applies to the tumour type.

Does a large ovarian mass automatically mean stage IV?

No. Stage depends on spread and other defined findings, not the diameter of the original mass alone.

What distinguishes IC1 from IC2?

IC1 involves surgical spill. IC2 involves rupture before surgery or tumour on the ovarian or tubal surface. The full pathology and operative findings determine the classification.

Can lymph-node spread be stage III without visible abdominal deposits?

Yes. IIIA1 describes the relevant retroperitoneal-node-only spread. The specialist must confirm the complete pattern and substage.

Is cancer on the liver the same as cancer inside it?

No. Capsule involvement can fall within stage IIIC, while growth in liver tissue is distant spread. The precise location matters.

Does fluid around a lung always mean stage IVA?

No. Stage IVA requires malignant cells in that fluid. Other causes of fluid and the complete staging findings need assessment.

Does five-year survival mean I can only live five years?

No. It is a statistical follow-up point, not a deadline. Relative survival also compares the cancer cohort with a comparable general population.

Why do two websites show different percentages?

They may use different diagnosis years, countries, tumour types, follow-up methods or stage groupings. Check those details before comparing them.

Are the percentages here my personal odds?

No. They describe US registry cohorts diagnosed in 2015–2021. The oncology team can explain which information is relevant to your particular diagnosis and care.

Does advanced disease mean there is nothing to discuss?

No. Treatment goals, symptom relief, support and possible trials depend on the disease and person. Ask the team about realistic options and what matters most to you.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
